CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models

Shengjing Liu ††thanks: ˜˜Equal contribution.    Feiyang Li11footnotemark: 1    Yuxuan Yang    Yile Wang ††thanks: ˜˜Corresponding author: wangyile@szu.edu.cn.    Hui Huang Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Software Engineering, Shenzhen University
Abstract

Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as “Wait”, “Alternatively”, and “Hmm”, suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%–25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%–1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results. Code is available at https://github.com/szu-tera/CALM.git.

1 Introduction

Large reasoning models (LRMs) such as OpenAI o1 OpenAI (2024) and DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025) have advanced rapidly and achieved strong performance on solving challenging mathematical and graduate-level science problems, largely owing to their long chain-of-thought (CoT; Wei et al., 2022) reasoning and test-time scaling Snell et al. (2025); Muennighoff et al. (2025). However, research reveals that LRMs could exhibit overthinking Su et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Cuadron et al. (2025), characterized by extensive redundant reasoning that not only fails to improve model performance but also results in considerable token waste and extra inference latency Gema et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026).

To reduce overthinking, recent efforts attempt to identify critical points during reasoning at which the model’s reasoning information is sufficient, so as to truncate the reasoning path by forcing the generation of the end-of-thinking token </think> and eliciting the final answer directly. For example, researchers have used consecutive trial-answer agreement Fu et al. (2024); Liu and Wang (2025) as a truncation signal, as shown in Figure 1(a).

We argue that although this truncation-based early-exiting approach can reduce token consumption, it still restricts the model’s inherent reasoning ability. We conduct a pilot study (§\lx@sectionsign 3.3) and find that the stopping signal is not necessarily indicative of final-answer stability, with even considerable gaps observed on certain datasets. The reason can be that subsequent thinking may still contain steps that help improve the reasoning outcome, such as reflection and verification (Guo et al., 2025). Meanwhile, interrupting the reasoning process severely suppresses the continuity of the model’s thinking, leading to incoherent reasoning context and a mismatch with the data and preferences encountered during training, thereby affecting the accuracy of the final answer (Koh et al., 2026; Wang and Zhu, 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Therefore, we attempt to answer the following question: How can LRMs naturally stop thinking when their reasoning progress is detected to be approaching saturation?

We begin with typical thinking words such as “Wait”, “Alternatively”, and “Hmm” Muennighoff et al. (2025), also termed as action transition point (ATP; Yang et al., 2026), and find that suppressing their generation probabilities can sustain generation while preserving accuracy (§\lx@sectionsign 3.3). The findings are also in line with recent work showing that ATP words do not genuinely reflect reasoning ability, but instead lead to lengthy reasoning steps Pandey et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2025); Yu et al. (2026). Therefore, we propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a simple yet effective inference-time decoding strategy for mitigating overthinking of LRMs, which consists of two steps: detecting consecutive answer agreement (§\lx@sectionsign 4.1) and action transition point logit masking (§\lx@sectionsign 4.2).

We evaluate on four advanced large reasoning models including DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen (7B, 14B, 32B) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Experiments across five mathematics and science benchmarks show that CALM outperforms recent baselines. In particular, CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%–25.0% while maintaining performance compared with full CoT, and achieves a slight accuracy gain of 0.07%–1.48% through mitigating redundant reasoning.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

1) Our pilot study shows that signals such as consecutive trial-answer agreement do not recover the completed-trace answer stably, revealing the limitations of truncation-based approaches, specifically their excessive reliance on local signals.

2) We propose CALM, a training-free decoding intervention method by suppressing the probability of typical thinking tokens to facilitate continual reasoning progress while reducing lengthy and redundant reasoning.

3) We evaluate two variants of CALM across four models and five benchmarks. Experimental results show that CALM substantially reduces redundant reasoning steps while outperforming recent baselines in terms of performance preservation.

2 Related Work

Overthinking of LRMs.

Recent work on overthinking of LRMs can be categorized into three types, as summarized in Table 1:

1) Training-based methods. Typical reinforcement learning methods include L1 (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025), which controls how long the model thinks through length penalties, S-GRPO (Dai et al., 2025), which evaluates the sufficiency of intermediate reasoning steps for early exiting, and ThinkPrune (Hou et al., 2026), which trains LRMs with an added token limit. For internal thought compression methods, LightThinker (Zhang et al., 2025) compresses intermediate thoughts into compact representations, while Li et al. (2026b) replaces selected low-entropy step with a special token [SKIP]. These methods incur prohibitive retraining overhead and cannot be deployed as plug-and-play interventions on frozen LRMs.

2) Prompt-based methods. Prompt-based methods encourage concise reasoning through prompt constraints. Chain of Draft (Xu et al., 2025) limits reasoning to short draft steps. Plan and Budget (Lin et al., 2026) assigns a length budget to the reasoning. Such constraints can be ignored on difficult problems or suppress necessary intermediate reasoning (Yu et al., 2025), so they are difficult to apply across diverse scenarios stably.

3) Inference-based methods. Reasoning truncation methods follow a “detect, truncate, early exit” pipeline. For example, Dynasor (Fu et al., 2024) probes trial answers at fixed token intervals and stops when consecutive probes agree. Answer Convergence (Liu and Wang, 2025) probes at reasoning-chunk boundaries and exits when consecutive answers match. TRACE (Li et al., 2026a) aggregates answer agreement and the confidence trajectory over a sliding window. REFRAIN (Sun et al., 2026) identifies steps that are both reflective and redundant. PUMA (Min et al., 2026) trains a detector to flag redundant steps and stops after verifying answer consistency and confidence. DEER (Yang et al., 2026) elicits a trial answer at transitions and exits when confidence exceeds a threshold.

These methods force the model to terminate its reasoning upon satisfaction of the stopping criterion, thereby restricting subsequent generation without token limitations. In contrast, we mitigate overthinking from the perspective of suppressing the probabilities of specific tokens in decoding space, yet maintain the capacity for sustained generation while reducing thinking redundancy.

Thinking Tokens in LRMs.

Muennighoff et al. (2025) try appending additional thinking tokens such as “Wait” and “Hmm” to enable test-time scaling. DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025) also demonstrates an “aha moment” after reinforcement learning training, which appears as self-reflection following stop words such as “Wait”. However, Liu et al. (2025) show that the phenomenon already exists in base models and does not reflect reasoning ability. Wang et al. (2025a) directly disables the generation of these words and find that it does not compromise the utility of multimodal models. Yu et al. (2026) classifies such words as anthropomorphic reflection markers and finds that these markers primarily affect how reasoning trajectories are organized on the surface and sampled. These works mainly focus on empirical findings and mechanistic analysis, whereas we design a decoding strategy that conditionally suppresses such thinking tokens in long reasoning chains, retains the model’s capacity for continuous generation, and practically mitigates overthinking in LRMs.

3 Preliminaries and Pilot Study

3.1 Task Formulation and Notations

Given a question QQ, an autoregressive reasoning model generates a chain-of-thought reasoning sequence S=(s1,…,sN)S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}), followed by a final answer yy. We segment the sequence into NN steps at natural paragraph or step boundaries, with the rules given in Appendix A. The task is to reduce unnecessary redundant reasoning steps while preserving the accuracy of answer yy. Let s1:ns_{1:n} denote the reasoning prefix up to step nn. Following the probing paradigm of prior early-exit studies Fu et al. (2024); Liu and Wang (2025), we sample an intermediate trial answer ana_{n} conditioned on s1:ns_{1:n} at each step boundary nn by appending an answer-inducing suffix on an independent decoding branch. This probing branch does not alter the original reasoning context. Consequently, each reasoning step sns_{n} is associated with a trial answer ana_{n}. The suffix strings are provided in Appendix B.

Tracking intermediate trial answers enables monitoring reasoning stability during generation. Notably, existing early-exit methods adopt consecutive trial answer agreement as a criterion to early-stop and truncate generation Fu et al. (2024); Liu and Wang (2025).

3.2 Action Transition Point

During long chain-of-thought generation, LRMs alternate among distinct thinking actions, such as approach exploration and procedural execution. Switches between these actions are typically indicated by explicit thinking tokens such as “Wait”. Following the naming by Yang et al. (2026), we formalize these tokens as action transition points (ATP) and denote their set by 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}}.

There is currently no rigorous definition of the ATP vocabulary. Following Wang et al. (2025a), we use three LRMs on five benchmarks to identify the sentence-initial words of different reasoning steps, and select the top 8 words to form the initial 𝒱ATPinit\mathcal{V}^{\rm init}_{\mathrm{ATP}} = {“So”,“Wait”, “But”,“Therefore”, “Alternatively”, “However”, “Maybe”,“Hmm”}. We find that reflection words such as “Wait”, “Alternatively”, and “Hmm” have been discussed in recent work Muennighoff et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025b); Yu et al. (2026) and these words may be highly correlated with redundant reasoning, and other control words regulate verification and thinking, thereby preserving the accuracy of long chain-of-thought reasoning. We therefore focus on three words 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}} = {“Wait”, “Alternatively”, and “Hmm”}, and we conduct vocabulary ablation in Section 6.2.

3.3 Reasoning Trace after Answer Agreement

We hypothesize that once tentative answer agreement is reached, subsequent ATP triggers predominantly degenerate into computational redundancy, needlessly bloating the reasoning trajectory. To examine this, we track the reasoning continuation starting from the first answer agreement. We conduct a pilot study on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B Guo et al. (2025) and OlympiadBench He et al. (2024) to investigate how accuracy changes with the mean number of continuation tokens after consecutive identical answers, comparing unconstrained vanilla CoT with a continuation that suppresses 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}} tokens after agreement. Detailed settings are given in Appendix C.

Figure 2 illustrates two key dynamics of this continuation. First, immediate truncation upon identical trial answers incurs a substantial accuracy gap. At the start of the continuation (x=0x=0), the probed trial answer achieves an accuracy of only 46.0%, falling 10.4 points below vanilla CoT (56.4%). Truncating immediately at this boundary severs downstream derivations and discards the opportunity for later revisions. Second, both continuations allow the model to conclude, while suppressing ATP tokens shortens the continuation. Suppressing 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}} after agreement saves 19.9% of post-agreement tokens while reaching a final accuracy comparable to Vanilla CoT.

4 Method

Grounded in the empirical findings in Section 3.3, we propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding-based method for mitigating overthinking.Rather than terminating generation early by truncating, CALM allows generation after detecting consecutive trial-answer agreement. Figure 3 illustrates the overall pipeline.

4.1 Detecting Consecutive Answer Agreement

At each step boundary nn, CALM obtains the current trial answer ana_{n} following the probing procedure described in Section 3. We monitor the sequence of trial answers to detect the earliest window in which the model outputs identical answers for kk consecutive steps. Formally, the consecutive-agreement indicator cnc_{n} and the agreement boundary step b⋆b^{\star} are defined as:

cn=𝟙[an=an−1=⋯=an−k+1],c_{n}=\mathbbm{1}[a_{n}=a_{n-1}=\cdots=a_{n-k+1}], (1)
b⋆=min⁡{n≥MSS:cn=1},b^{\star}=\min\{n\geq{\rm MSS}:c_{n}=1\}, (2)

where 𝟙\mathbbm{1}[⋅\cdot] denotes the indicator function and MSS\rm{MSS} is the minimum stop step. If the trial answers never reach kk consecutive matches during generation, then b⋆=∞b^{\star}=\infty and the reasoning trajectory remains entirely unmodified.

4.2 Action Transition Point Logit Masking

After obtaining the agreement boundary b⋆b^{\star}, CALM adds a masking bias to the logits of candidate tokens that match 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}}. Formally, at decoding position tt within the reasoning steps, let hth_{t} denote the final hidden state and WLMW_{\mathrm{LM}} the vocabulary projection weight of the LM Head. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the model’s token vocabulary. For each candidate token v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, the raw logit is ℓt(v)=[WLMht]idx:v\ell_{t}(v)=[W_{\mathrm{LM}}h_{t}]_{{\rm idx}:v}, to which we add a bias bt​(v)b_{t}(v) for logit masking:

ℓt​(v)\displaystyle\ell_{t}(v) =[WLMht]idx:v,\displaystyle=[W_{\mathrm{LM}}h_{t}]_{{\rm idx}:v}, (3)
ℓ~t​(v)\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{t}(v) =ℓt​(v)+bt​(v),\displaystyle=\ell_{t}(v)+b_{t}(v),

where idx:v{{\rm idx}:v} denotes the index of v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}. Let tt be a token position and n⁡(t)n(t) be the corresponding reasoning step. We investigate two masking strategies for the bias term bt​(v)b_{t}(v):

Hard Masking employs a constant value to strictly prohibit ATP tokens once the agreement boundary is crossed:

bt​(v)={−∞if n(t)>b⋆,v∈ℬt,0otherwise,b_{t}(v)=\begin{cases}-\infty&\text{if }n(t)>b^{\star},\,v\in\mathcal{B}_{t},\\ 0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (4)

where ℬt⊆𝒱\mathcal{B}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{V} is the set of token ids that complete an ATP surface form under the current prefix. The surface forms and the matching rules are given in Appendix D. Vocabulary ablations are reported in Section 6.2.

Soft Masking adopts an adaptive progressive penalty through decisive damping rather than a rigid ban. Let c⁡(t)c(t) denote the occurrence count of ATP strings completed after b⋆b^{\star} and before position tt, with penalty η⁡(c)=−10​(1−ρc)\eta(c)=-10(1-\rho^{c}) for 0<ρ<10<\rho<1:

bt​(v)={η⁡(c⁡(t))if n(t)>b⋆,v∈ℬt,0otherwise,b_{t}(v)=\begin{cases}\eta(c(t))&\text{if }n(t)>b^{\star},\,v\in\mathcal{B}_{t},\\ 0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (5)

where the penalty is 00 when c⁡(t)=0c(t)=0, and smoothly approaches −10-10 as c⁡(t)c(t) accumulates. Under a softmax operation, a value of −10-10 reduces an affected token’s relative weight by a factor of about e−10≈4.5×10−5e^{-10}\approx 4.5\times 10^{-5}. The sensitivity of hyperparameter ρ\rho is shown in Section 6.3.

After applying probability suppression to ATP tokens, CALM enables continual decoding without truncation or imposing additional token limits. We evaluate both CALM (soft) with progressive penalty and CALM (hard) with constant masking in our main experiments.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on five reasoning benchmarks that span several difficulty levels: four mathematical benchmarks including MATH-500 Lightman et al. (2024), OlympiadBench He et al. (2024), AIME 2025 MAA Committees (2025), and AMC 2023 AI-MO (2024), and one scientific reasoning benchmark:GPQA-Diamond Rein et al. (2024).

Models.

Four DeepSeek models are used in main experiments, including DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen (7B, 14B, and 32B) Guo et al. (2025) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. For additional models Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B Bercovich et al. (2025), Qwen3 (4B, 8B, 30B-A3B, 32B) Yang et al. (2025), and QwQ-32B Qwen Team (2025), results are given in Appendix E.

Baselines.

To make a fair evaluation, we compare with inference-based methods including Answer Convergence (Ans. Conv.; Liu and Wang, 2025), Dynasor Fu et al. (2024), TRACE Li et al. (2026a), PUMA Min et al. (2026), and DEER Yang et al. (2026). We obtain and report the results based on their open-source version.

Evaluation Metrics.

We report accuracy (Acc) and average generated tokens (Tok). Overall, we additionally report token efficiency (TE), using the OckScore Du et al. (2025) defined as accuracy minus λ​ln⁡(T/C+1)\lambda\ln(T/C+1), with λ=10\lambda=10, C=10,000C=10{,}000, natural logarithm, accuracy in percentage points, and TT the average token count.

Implementation Details.

All experiments use 4 NVIDIA L40 GPUs, and all methods run under one vLLM host. The main generation budget is 32,76832{,}768 tokens. If this budget ends before the thought closes, the answer continuation is at most 2,0482{,}048 tokens. Each reported cell is the mean over seeds 42, 0, and 1. The main experiments set the window length to k=4k=4, and the minimum stop step is MSS=10\mathrm{MSS}=10, so b⋆b^{\star} is no earlier than step 10. Section 6.3 compares other lengths. We provide a more detailed analysis at Appendix F.

5.2 Main Results

Overall Performance.

As shown in Table 2, CALM achieves the highest overall TE on all four backbones. Relative to Full CoT, CALM (Hard) reduces overall token usage by 18.6%18.6\%–25.0%25.0\%, with overall accuracy 0.070.07–1.481.48 points higher. It also achieves higher overall accuracy with fewer tokens than both PUMA and DEER on every backbone. Both CALM variants reduce token usage across all 20 model–benchmark settings, although their effects on accuracy vary across tasks. Table 6 in Appendix E also presents results on six additional models, where CALM similarly reduces token consumption by 14%14\%–18.9%18.9\% and achieves better accuracy and token efficiency than other baselines.

Comparison with Early-Exit Methods.

Early-exit baselines exhibit different accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Answer Convergence reduces overall token usage by 82.7%82.7\%–88.3%88.3\%, but lowers overall accuracy by 17.3917.39–35.9335.93 percentage points relative to Full CoT. In contrast, DEER increases token usage by 0.7%0.7\%–2.3%2.3\% on GPQA-Diamond for the three Qwen backbones, because its high threshold almost never triggers early exit on GPQA-Diamond and trial-answer probing adds tokens. In Appendix G, we provide detailed statistics on the proportion of this early-stopping signal (stop coverage) and find that CALM intervenes on more questions than PUMA and DEER truncate in most settings, which helps explain the larger token reductions on some benchmarks. Overall, the superiority of CALM comes from the suppression of ATP after consecutive identical answers, while subsequent deduction and correction continue without degrading intermediate reasoning quality.

Soft vs. Hard Masking.

Hard masking achieves lower overall token usage than soft masking on all four backbones, whereas their accuracy advantage depends on the backbone. Soft masking attains the highest overall accuracy on Qwen-7B and Qwen-14B, reaching 66.47%66.47\% and 72.75%72.75\%, respectively, while reducing overall token usage by 21.0%21.0\% and 14.3%14.3\% relative to Full CoT. Hard masking achieves even higher overall accuracy and TE on Qwen-32B and Llama-8B. Also, it consistently provides greater overall token savings, while the preferred variant for accuracy depends on the backbone. Overall, both strategies achieve better results across all evaluated model architectures, demonstrating the effectiveness of decoding-based intervention.

Scales and Domains.

The benefits of CALM generalize across model capacities and problem distributions. Across the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen family spanning 7B to 32B parameters, generation length is shortened while accuracy stays close to full CoT. The largest reduction is 25.0%25.0\% on the 7B model. The same pattern appears on competition mathematics (MATH-500, OlympiadBench, and AIME 2025) and on GPQA-Diamond, demonstrating the applicability of our method across diverse challenging reasoning tasks.

6 Analysis

We conduct further analysis of our method and CALM (Soft) is used unless otherwise noted.

6.1 Right-to-Wrong Transitions

A critical risk of reducing overthinking is that early intervention may cause errors on questions that Full CoT answers correctly. We examine the degradation rate by tracking the share of all questions on which Full CoT is correct and the method is incorrect. Figure 4 shows the results and we find that: 1) Premature truncation corrupts effective reasoning. Truncation-based early-exit baselines such as Dynasor and DEER suffer from high degradation rates. Their risk is that stopping once a local signal is met can leave out later steps that may still revise the answer. 2) Our method Effectively Mitigates Performance Degradation. By keeping the generation trajectory open, CALM substantially mitigates this corruption of performance with the lowest degradation rate.

6.2 Ablation on ATP Vocabulary

We compare the results of suppressing different tokens in the ATP vocabulary 𝒱ATP\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ATP}}. Results on MATH-500 by using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B are shown in Table 3. We first find that although suppressing all eight words in 𝒱ATPfull\mathcal{V}^{\rm full}_{\mathrm{ATP}} significantly reduces token length (3,316 vs. 3,847), it also decreases accuracy by 2 percentage points. Under individual suppression, both reflection and connective control tokens can almost reduce tokens, but suppressing control tokens leads to performance degradation, resulting in lower overall token efficiency, whereas suppressing anthropomorphic tokens alone maintains accuracy. We achieve the best result of 89.77 when jointly suppressing the reflection words “Wait”, “Alternatively”, and “Hmm”. These results illustrate the roles of different thinking tokens in the ATP vocabulary.

6.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity

We evaluate how hyperparameters balance reasoning completeness and token efficiency.

Damping Dynamics via Soft Decay ρ\rho. Table 4 shows the impact of different values of the progressive penalty factor ρ\rho. We observe that ρ=0.98\rho=0.98 achieves the highest accuracy, the shortest length, and the highest TE (62.0562.05). A steeper decay (ρ=0.95\rho=0.95) accumulates the penalty too fast, leading to an accuracy drop. Milder settings (ρ≥0.99\rho\geq 0.99) accumulate the penalty more slowly and exert weaker damping, failing to curb the generation length inflated by redundant verification.

Impact of the Consistency Window Size kk. As shown in Figure 5, the performance of CALM varies by only 1.54 percentage points across window lengths k∈{1,…,6}k\in\{1,\ldots,6\}. The impact on tokens is slightly greater, while all settings substantially reduce token usage relative to Full CoT. We adopt k=4k=4 as the default, as it achieves the highest accuracy of 65.73% with 6,192 tokens, providing a favorable balance between accuracy and efficiency.

6.4 Comparison through LLM-as-a-Judge

Beyond accuracy and efficiency comparisons, we evaluate reasoning-chain quality using Qwen3.5-397B-A17B through LLM-as-a-judge along dimensions of completeness, coherence, conciseness, and justification. Results in Table 5 show that CALM achieves a higher average than the other methods and scores higher than them on completeness, coherence, and justification. In particular, after consecutive answer agreement, Full CoT still triggers ATP repeatedly, and unresolved contradictions and derivations abandoned midway make its completeness and justification lower than those of CALM. The detailed setup and a few case studies are given in Appendix I and Appendix J, respectively.

7 Conclusion

We proposed consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a simple yet effective training-free decoding strategy that detects consecutive answer agreement and then suppresses the logits of action transition point tokens to reduce redundant reasoning while preserving generation continuity. Extensive experiments on ten advanced reasoning models and five benchmarks show that CALM substantially reduces token usage while maintaining or even slightly improving accuracy relative to full CoT, offering a practical decoding-space solution to overthinking, and future work may explore adaptive masking policies, broader task domains, and combinations with reinforcement-learning or prompt-based efficiency methods.

Limitations

CALM reduces generation length while keeping accuracy close to full chain-of-thought. Two limitations remain open for future work.First, the main experiments use one window length kk for every item, without varying it by problem. Adapting the window length or the logit penalty to each instance, for example from token-level entropy, is a direction for future work. Second, the evaluation in this paper covers textual mathematics and science reasoning. Whether these transition tokens are used to handle external feedback in tool-use or multimodal settings is not tested here. Extending the suppression to those settings would require separating transitions that still serve a function from the meaningless exploration or verification that follows consecutive identical answers.

Appendix A Reasoning Step Segmentation

Trial answers are probed at the level of reasoning steps, so the thought before ⟨/think⟩\langle/\mathrm{think}\rangle is segmented by the deterministic, lightweight procedure of PUMA Min et al. (2026). Given the raw reasoning text, we first split the chain at blank-line boundaries, which preserves the model’s natural paragraph structure. We then assign each paragraph a coarse semantic role using simple string-level cues, such as problem setup, calculation, doubt, verification, conclusion, or general reasoning. These labels are not used as model inputs; they only guide how adjacent paragraphs are grouped into larger reasoning steps.

The merging stage balances semantic coherence and step length. Enumerated paragraphs or major semantic transitions are treated as natural step boundaries, while short adjacent paragraphs with compatible roles are merged when doing so preserves coherence. We use a target step length range of [Lmin,Lmax]=[200,1000][L_{\min},L_{\max}]=[200,1000] characters, and tiny trailing segments are merged into the preceding step. This merged span is one reasoning step, and the trial answer is probed at its boundary.

Appendix B Trial Answer Inducing Suffix

For mathematics and contest problems, the answer-inducing suffix is:

\n**Final Answer**\n\nThe final answer is \boxed.

For GPQA-Diamond, the suffix is:

\n**Final Answer**\n\nThe answer choice is \boxed.

Before two trial answers are compared, the boxed strings are normalized by lowercasing, deleting whitespace, and stripping formatting macros.

Appendix C Detailed Settings in Pilot Study

Samples.

Figure 2 uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on OlympiadBench . Vanilla CoT and ATP suppression use the same questions. Only questions whose trial answers are identical for four consecutive steps for the first time are included, 633 of the 675 questions. Accuracy and tokens use these 633 questions as a fixed denominator and give each question equal weight. The dashed line is the completed vanilla CoT accuracy on these questions.

Horizontal Axis.

The horizontal axis is zero when the four consecutive identical trial answers end. The horizontal coordinate after that point is the mean, over the 633 questions, of the tokens added at each step after agreement. A question that has already stopped remains at the tokens it actually added after agreement. After ⟨/think⟩\langle/\mathrm{think}\rangle, the curve continues only once every included question has finished its thought, and that segment counts ⟨/think⟩\langle/\mathrm{think}\rangle together with the following text.

Vertical Axis.

At that position, accuracy is the fraction of the 633 questions whose trial answer is correct.The trial answer is produced by continuing from that prefix for at most 30 tokens and closing the answer in \boxed{}.A finished question keeps its last correctness.

Appendix H Additional Right-to-Wrong Rates

Figure 6 extends Figure 4 to four models on MATH-500. The rate is the share of questions that full CoT answers correctly and the method answers incorrectly. CALM Soft is the lowest among Dynasor, DEER, PUMA, and CALM on every panel. These additional results demonstrate the stability of our method, whereas other truncation-based methods are indeed prone to depriving the model of opportunities for subsequent correction.

Appendix I Settings for LLM-as-a-Judge

We evaluate the quality of retained reasoning chains with an LLM judge. The goal is to measure whether the retained chain remains a readable and sufficient derivation, beyond final-answer accuracy.

Judge Model and Protocol.

The judge is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, called at temperature 0 with at most 1,024 output tokens. Each call receives the problem, the retained reasoning, and the answer submitted by that method. The judge writes a one-sentence rationale before the scores.

Scope.

The evaluated chains are generations of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on MATH-500. We randomly draw 60 questions, and every method is scored on these 60 questions. The model’s input is the problem, the retained reasoning, and the submitted answer. When a method stops early, the retained reasoning ends at that stop; otherwise it is the full reasoning.

Rubric.

Each chain is scored from 10 to 100 in steps of 10 on completeness, coherence, conciseness, and justification, following the four dimensions of PUMA Min et al. (2026). Completeness asks whether the essential steps from the problem to the stated answer are present. Coherence asks whether the progression is connected and whether revisions are resolved. Conciseness asks whether repetition or unproductive detours are present, and missing steps are scored under completeness and justification instead. Justification asks whether the written derivation supports the stated answer. The prompt states the anchors at 100, 70, 40, and 10.
